name: Bonnie Prudden myotherapy

card.summary: A trigger-point pressure and corrective-exercise method from the 1970s that practitioners use to release tight muscles and ease pain, supporting posture and comfortable training.
card.note: Based on the broader trigger-point concept, which researchers describe as debated.

quick.overview:
Bonnie Prudden myotherapy is a method developed by American fitness pioneer Bonnie Prudden (1914-2011) in 1976. It combines pressure on tender spots in muscle (trigger points) with specific exercises, with the stated aim of relaxing muscle spasm, improving circulation and relieving pain [1].

Its appearance payoff runs through posture and movement: looser, less painful muscles make it easier to stand, move and train comfortably, which supports a straighter frame and more consistent exercise. Research on trigger-point therapy in general exists, but studies of Prudden's own method are not part of the published literature found here.
quick.how: Practitioners locate sore points in a muscle, apply sustained pressure, and then prescribe stretching or corrective exercises. People also use Prudden's books for self-treatment.
quick.risks: Pressure on tender muscle can be uncomfortable and cause temporary soreness. Persistent or unexplained pain is generally something clinicians recommend having assessed.

lead: Bonnie Prudden myotherapy is a manual and exercise method created by the American fitness figure Bonnie Prudden, who is credited with coining the term and developing the practice in 1976. Prudden described it as a method of relaxing muscle spasm, improving circulation and alleviating pain [1].

In a looks context, people use myotherapy-style trigger-point work to release tight muscles that pull on posture, such as the neck, shoulders and back, and to keep training comfortable. The chain runs from less muscle tension to better posture and more consistent exercise.

Prudden was a dancer, rock climber, and youth-fitness advocate; with physician Hans Kraus she presented Kraus-Weber test results to the Eisenhower White House in 1955 [1]. Her 1980 book Pain Erasure: The Bonnie Prudden Way was a New York Times best seller [1].

chain: More consistent exercise and a straighter frame
angle.text: Practitioners use pressure on trigger points plus corrective exercises to loosen tight muscles. Looser muscles make good posture and regular training more comfortable.

paras: Prudden's own description is a method of relaxing muscle spasm, improving circulation and relieving pain through work on trigger points combined with corrective exercise [1]. Trigger points, in the wider literature, are described as hyperirritable spots in skeletal muscle, often felt as nodules in taut bands, where pressure can cause local tenderness or referred pain [2].

Prudden trained in dance and gymnastics, climbed extensively in the Shawangunks in the 1940s and 1950s, and opened an Institute for Physical Fitness in White Plains, New York, in 1954 [1]. She wrote a Sports Illustrated column from 1957 to 1960 and hosted a television show [1]. Myotherapy was her later contribution, developed in 1976 [1]. The trigger-point idea she built on was popularised in the mid-20th century by physician Janet Travell [2].

No studies found on Prudden myotherapy specifically. Studies of broader trigger-point therapy are described as limited: a summary of the literature reports moderate evidence of short-term relief from manual therapy, dry needling found no more effective than placebo in a 2019 review, and scarce evidence for exercise, with the trigger-point concept itself described as controversial [2]. A 2015 critical review argued the concept lacks scientific basis, and practitioners published a rebuttal [2].

Sustained pressure on sore muscle can cause temporary discomfort. Wikipedia notes that Prudden's biographical article relies heavily on primary sources, including her own books and her business website [1].

Prudden and Hans Kraus present youth fitness findings to the Eisenhower White House [1].
